solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

R058-01.notes: Passage moves from the old 3-decade explanation, to the 2002 revision (second enzyme), to what it enabled (tearless onions), plus kitchen tips and defense. A: passage only reports GM onions weren't sold; no advocacy. C: garlic is used as a chemical contrast, not a cooking preference. D: kitchen methods are one paragraph only, too narrow.

R058-02.notes: P2: 'a second enzyme seizes most of it [the unstable intermediate] first and converts it into a volatile compound that is the real irritant.' A: that is alliinase's job. B: in garlic the intermediate reacts with itself, no enzyme. C: reverses the process; the irritant is the product, and flavor compounds come from the alternate path.

R058-03.notes: 'The trouble was that alliinase does much the same work in garlic, and garlic does not make people cry' - an anomaly the old alliinase-only account could not explain. B: contradicts text (alliinase works in garlic). C: passage says the corresponding compound, i.e., same pathway; no different starting material. D: no claim about cook preference.

R058-04.notes: Enzyme grabs the intermediate before it can react with itself = takes hold of. A: wrong sense of 'seize' (grasp an idea). B: confiscate implies legal/authority removal. D: 'attacks suddenly' is the plausible trap (seize as in an attack/fit), but the enzyme captures and converts; no attack.

R058-05.notes: P3: switching off the second enzyme lets the intermediate 'follow the garlic-like path,' and P4 reports higher levels of other flavor-associated sulfur compounds. A: chilling is irrelevant to flavor. B: alliinase doesn't produce the stored compounds; it breaks them down, and no increase is mentioned. C: contradicts the premise - if the irritant were the flavor source, removing it would make the onion bland.

R058-06.notes: Nearly verbatim from P4: 'genetically modified onions faced regulatory and consumer hurdles.' B: they released 'far less' irritant. C: analysis found higher flavor compounds. D: the bred onion was from a Japanese company, sold in Japan, in the 2010s.

R058-07.notes: Sentence states the tricks don't stop the reaction but reduce how much irritant forms/arrives - clarifies their actual effect and limit. A: the paragraph says the advice 'makes sense' chemically; it does have an effect. C: no new method introduced; next paragraph turns to defense. D: no mention of the bred onions there.

R058-08.notes: Sharp knife works by crushing fewer cells, releasing less starting material; fewer, cleaner cuts likewise rupture fewer cells. A: refrigerating = chilling, which works by slowing enzymes/evaporation (different reason). B: open window carries irritant away (delivery, not formation). D: distance reduces how much arrives, same category as B. Application item; the 'cleaner' wording slightly echoes 'sharp' but still requires the cell-damage reasoning.

R058-09.notes: Final paragraph: chemistry 'appears to be a defense' against animals that bite the bulb; affecting cooks is incidental. A: no breeding for irritant; contradicts 'accident.' B: P5 says no trick stops the reaction. C: passage says the 2002 work explained the process.

R058-10.notes: P1: 'Cutting ruptures the cells, the two meet, and a chain of reactions begins' - this initiates the sequence. B: a later (second-enzyme) step. C: the final step, after the irritant forms. D: the garlic path, and it comes after alliinase acts anyway.

R058-11.notes: 'Worked until the light went thin' on a gray late-October afternoon = daylight grew faint/dim. A and C: physical-width senses of thin that don't apply to light. D: sharp is the opposite of fading light.

R058-12.notes: 'If I wrote the reason down, it would come out smaller than it was' = putting it in words would diminish something meaningful. A: daughter never involved in the letter. B: narrator says 'I thought I knew'; no suggestion of a wrong guess. C: the concern is diminishing the meaning, not proving attentiveness.

R058-13.notes: First-person 'I,' the fourteen-year-old neighbor kneeling with the trowel, telling the story in past tense through April. A: Halvorsen is 'he,' and never explains. B: the mother is observed from the narrator's window. D: narrator explicitly doesn't know Halvorsen's reasons ('I kept waiting for him to explain'), so not omniscient.
